clinicalPearls: WAGR is a contiguous gene deletion syndrome of chromosome 11p13 encompassing loss of PAX6 (aniridia) and the adjacent WT1 tumour-suppressor gene (Wilms tumour predisposition and genitourinary maldevelopment).
Any infant with sporadic aniridia, particularly bilateral, should have genetic testing for an 11p13/WT1 deletion, because this single finding determines lifelong Wilms tumour risk.
Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumour) risk is substantially raised, so structured renal ultrasound surveillance is recommended through early childhood.
Genitourinary anomalies such as cryptorchidism, hypospadias, ambiguous genitalia and streak or dysgenetic gonads reflect WT1 haploinsufficiency and carry a gonadoblastoma risk.
WT1 involvement also predisposes to progressive nephropathy (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis) and later renal failure, sometimes emerging after the cancer-surveillance years.
Aniridia is rarely an isolated absent iris; associated foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, glaucoma, cataract and keratopathy all threaten vision.
The WAGRO variant adds obesity and hyperphagia, attributed to a more telomeric deletion involving the BDNF gene.
Chromosomal microarray defines the extent of the deletion and correlates with phenotype severity, guiding surveillance and genetic counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: WAGR syndrome arises from a heterozygous, usually de novo, contiguous gene deletion of the short arm of chromosome 11 at band 11p13. The deleted interval spans several genes; loss of one PAX6 allele disrupts the master transcriptional regulator of eye development, producing aniridia and other ocular malformations, while haploinsufficiency of the neighbouring WT1 gene, which is essential for normal kidney and gonad differentiation, drives predisposition to Wilms tumour and to genitourinary and gonadal maldevelopment. Because WT1 acts as a tumour suppressor, a somatic second hit within surviving nephrogenic rests precipitates nephroblastoma, and the same WT1 loss underlies a distinct glomerulopathy that can progress to renal failure. The size of the deletion determines the phenotype: larger deletions extending telomerically to include the BDNF locus add childhood-onset obesity, hyperphagia and more pronounced neurobehavioural difficulties (the WAGRO variant), whereas the degree of intellectual disability varies with the total gene content lost.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated PAX6-related aniridia without WT1 involvement
Denys-Drash syndrome (WT1 point mutation with nephropathy, Wilms tumour and disorders of sex development)
Frasier syndrome (WT1 intronic mutation with progressive glomerulosclerosis and gonadoblastoma)
Gillespie syndrome (partial aniridia with cerebellar ataxia and intellectual disability)
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (overgrowth with Wilms tumour predisposition)
Other anterior segment dysgenesis such as Peters anomaly or Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum
Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome (overgrowth with embryonal tumour risk)
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to detect and define the extent of the 11p13 deletion
FISH or targeted analysis of the WT1/PAX6 region and karyotype
Serial renal ultrasound surveillance for early detection of Wilms tumour
Comprehensive ophthalmological assessment including slit-lamp, intraocular pressure and fundoscopy for foveal hypoplasia
Renal function tests and urinalysis for proteinuria to monitor for nephropathy
Pelvic and gonadal imaging with endocrine assessment for genitourinary anomalies and gonadoblastoma risk
redFlags: A new palpable abdominal mass or haematuria suggesting Wilms tumour
Proteinuria progressing towards nephrotic range, indicating WT1-related nephropathy and possible renal failure
Raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma threatening remaining vision
Features of gonadoblastoma arising within dysgenetic gonads
reference.prognosis: With structured renal surveillance Wilms tumours are usually detected early and are highly curable, but long-term outlook is tempered by the risk of progressive renal insufficiency, visual impairment from aniridia-related complications and variable intellectual disability. Life expectancy depends largely on renal and oncological outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming sporadic aniridia is isolated and thereby missing the Wilms tumour risk that mandates WT1 testing.
Discontinuing renal ultrasound surveillance too early in childhood.
Overlooking late-onset nephropathy and progressive renal failure that can appear after the tumour-surveillance period.
Failing to recognise gonadoblastoma risk in dysgenetic gonads.
Attributing developmental delay solely to visual impairment rather than the underlying deletion.
references: Principles and practice of medical genetics
management: Undertake structured renal ultrasound surveillance through early childhood for Wilms tumour, treating detected tumours with nephrectomy and chemotherapy
Manage aniridia-related eye disease with intraocular-pressure-lowering therapy or surgery for glaucoma, cataract surgery, tinted UV-protective lenses and low-vision support

Monitor renal function and urinary protein, using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker for proteinuric nephropathy and planning dialysis or transplantation for progression to renal failure
Correct genitourinary anomalies with orchidopexy or hypospadias repair, and remove dysgenetic or streak gonads to pre-empt gonadoblastoma
Provide developmental, educational and behavioural support for intellectual disability
Offer genetic counselling for the usually de novo 11p13 contiguous gene deletion
Coordinate lifelong care through a multidisciplinary team spanning oncology, nephrology, ophthalmology and clinical genetics
